reference_answer: Failure to comply, or failure to obtain permission for re-enrollment, may be a basis for denying re-enrollment, or may be treated as a violation of the Code and may result in expulsion or denial of academic credit during that period.

question: At Stanford, does a student still violate the Honor Code if they did not mean to, but a reasonable person should have known the activity was wrong?
reference_answer: Yes. Even where a Judicial Panel finds no willful intent, the student still violates the Honor Code if a reasonable person in their situation should have been aware that the activity was wrong.

question: When may the University of Glasgow end the Student Contract because of government sanctions, and on what date does it end?
reference_answer: Where your participation is affected by government-imposed sanctions or intervention on national-security grounds and the University cannot vary the programme or find an alternative, the Contract ends on the date the University withdraws you as a student.

question: For the purposes of the Stanford Student Judicial Charter, who counts as a “student”?
reference_answer: Any person who has accepted an offer of admission, or for whom the University maintains educational records under FERPA, and — for degree-seeking individuals — who has not yet been awarded their current degree. For some time we have been invoking a much narrower jurisdictional scope. The current scope is those students enrolled in Stanford degree-seeking programs or visiting/exchange students here under an agreement with their home institutions. question: How does Stanford’s Honor Code guidance define plagiarism?
reference_answer: As the use, without reasonable and appropriate credit to or acknowledgement of the author or source, of another person’s original work — whether that work is code, formulas, ideas, language, research, strategies, writing or other forms.

clauses.quote_evidence:
In the spring of 1977, the Student Conduct Legislative Council authored and adopted the following guidelines to assist students and faculty in understanding their rights and obligations under the University's Honor Code. The most recent revisions to the original text were adopted in the Winter of 2002 by the Board on Judicial Affairs.
In order to clarify and reaffirm what is regarded as plagiarism, the Board on Judicial Affairs provided the following statement in its Guidance on the Standard Sanction adopted on May 24, 2011: "For purposes of the Stanford University Honor Code, plagiarism is defined as the use, without giving reasonable and appropriate credit to or acknowledging the author or source, of another person's original work, whether such work is made up of code, formulas, ideas, language, research, strategies, writing or other form(s). Moreover, verbatim text from another source must always be put in (or within) quotation marks.”

question: At Glasgow, how long should conduct procedures normally take, and when may that timescale be extended?
reference_answer: Normally no more than 90 working days from the start of the investigation to the conclusion of any appeal meeting. Extensions may be needed for complex cases or circumstances beyond the University’s reasonable control, and academic cases may take longer at busy times of year.

clauses.quote_evidence: 33.56 Schools are expected to make referrals in a timely manner. Conduct procedures will then proceed without undue delay and where possible will not normally take more than 90 working days from the start of the investigation into an allegation to the conclusion of any appeal meeting. Extensions to this timescale may be required if, for example, the case is particularly complex, or due to other circumstances beyond the reasonable control of the University. Note that at certain times of year academic cases may take longer than 90 working days due to the increased number of referrals and the need to prioritise graduating students. Relevant parties will be informed of likely timescales and updated where delays are necessary or otherwise occur.

question: Under the Glasgow Code, what rights does a student facing misconduct allegations have?
reference_answer: To be informed of the allegations, to be heard, to support, and to appeal; all parties are treated with dignity and respect, and cases are considered objectively by competent, impartial investigators and decision makers.

clauses.quote_evidence: 33.8 The University will aim to treat all its students fairly under this Code and to adhere to the principles of natural justice. All parties will be treated with dignity and respect, and implementation of this Code will be sensitive to protected characteristics with reasonable adjustments made if required.[2] All students against whom allegations of misconduct are taken forward under this Code will be informed of the allegations against them, and will have the right to be heard, the right to support, and the rights of appeal, as set out in this Code. University of Glasgow students making allegations will have the right to receive support as set out in this Code. Cases will be considered objectively by investigators and decision makers who are competent and impartial.

question: In the MIT course, how much do the problem sets count, and are late problem sets accepted?
reference_answer: Eight problem sets are mandatory, each graded and returned; the best seven count for 25% of the final grade. Late problem sets are not accepted for any reason.

There will be eight mandatory problem sets which will be individually graded and returned to the students. question: When deciding whether a concern should go forward, what may the Director do at Berkeley, and what is that role not?

question: When should an instructor enter a P grade, and does a grade change have to be filed later?
reference_answer: For a course that extends beyond one term, such as a graduate research or thesis course, or for a series of related courses where a later grade replaces an earlier one. The Registrar then administratively replaces the P grade with the awarded grade, so no grade change is needed.

clauses.quote_evidence:
Enter a P grade for a student in a course that extends beyond one term (i.e. a graduate student in a research or thesis course). When you enter a final grade at the end of the course, the Office of the Registrar will administratively replace the P grade with the awarded grade; you will not need to complete a grade change.
You would also use a P grade for a student who is enrolled in a series of related courses in which the grade for an earlier course will be replaced by the grade for a later course (i.e. the PSYCH 681/PSYCH 682 series). When you enter a final grade for the last course, the Office of the Registrar will administratively replace the P grade(s) in the earlier course(s) with the new grade; you will not need to complete a grade change for the earlier course(s).

question: After Boston University finds a student responsible, what appeal route is open to them?
reference_answer: They may request a hearing before a UBSC panel, or waive the hearing and appeal directly to the Provost. question: At Glasgow, who appoints the Assessment Officer for a course and what does that role cover?
reference_answer: The Head of School appoints a member of academic or senior administrative staff as Assessment Officer for each course. The role includes collating the provisional results and ensuring they are accurately reported to the Board of Examiners, reporting on the conduct of the assessment procedure, and ensuring examiners are conversant with the learning outcomes.
